title: Boat Detailing Invoice Template
subtitle: An invoice pre-filled for boat detailers — wash and full-detail packages by the foot, compound and wax, teak refinishing, canvas and isenglass care, plus marina travel and haul-out fees. Download as Excel (auto-calculating), Word, or PDF.
taxHint: Look up your state's sales tax rate
paymentTerms: Due on completion at the dock. Seasonal wash-plan customers: invoiced monthly, Net 14.
notes: Thank you for your business. Weekly and bi-weekly wash plans available — seasonal rates quoted at the dock. Haul-out, lift, and yard fees billed at pass-through cost. Ask about ceramic coating for a full-season gloss.

features: Auto-calculating tax formulas in Excel — just enter your state rate
Pre-filled marine line items — per-foot packages, teak by the foot, canvas by the piece, haul-out pass-through

Travel and haul-out as visible lines — on-site work costs more than shop work, and the invoice shows why

faqs.q: What should I include on a boat detailing invoice?
faqs.a: Your business details, the client's name, and enough boat identification to pick it out of a crowded marina: year, make, length overall (LOA), and slip number. Break the work into hull, deck, and interior lines priced by the foot, list specialty work (teak, canvas, isenglass) separately with units, and note the products used — compound versus polish versus ceramic — plus cure times. Marina travel and any haul-out yard fee go on their own pass-through lines.

faqs.q: How much should I charge for boat detailing?
faqs.a: A basic wash runs $2–$5 per foot of LOA ($50–$120 for a typical 24 ft boat). Full details price at $15–$30 per foot — a 20 ft bowrider lands around $300–$600 and a 30 ft cruiser $600–$1,200. Compounding and waxing adds $8–$15 per foot, teak refinishing runs $25–$50 per linear foot, and canvas or isenglass cleaning is $50–$150 per piece. Monthly hull cleaning by a diver runs $3–$5 per foot.

faqs.q: Do boat detailers charge by the foot or by the job?
faqs.a: By the foot for recurring work — washes, bottom details, seasonal packages — because LOA predicts labor almost perfectly. Flat 'by the job' pricing makes sense only after seeing the boat: a salt-caked fishing boat with three years of oxidation is a different job than a freshwater cabin cruiser of the same length. Most detailers quote per foot with a $150–$250 minimum, then upcharge for heavy oxidation or neglected interiors.

faqs.q: Should I charge extra to work at the marina or haul-out?
faqs.a: Yes — as separate lines. Travel to the marina bills as a field-service trip ($50–$100 typical), and any haul-out, lift, or blocking fee the yard charges should pass through at cost with 'pass-through' written next to it. Customers accept these charges when they see them quoted up front; they dispute them when they appear as a lump sum after the work is done.

faqs.q: Is this template free to use?
faqs.a: Yes. All three formats (PDF, Word, Excel) are free to download with no email required.

faqs.q: Does the Excel version calculate tax automatically?
faqs.a: Yes. Enter your quantity and rate per line, and the subtotal, tax and total update automatically. Leave the tax rate blank if detailing services are not taxable in your state.

faqs.q: How do I price boat detailing when the owner asks 'how much for a detail'?
faqs.a: Answer with the length tier plus condition, never a single number. Ask for the length overall (LOA), whether it has been in salt water, and how long since the last compound. A 24 ft freshwater bowrider in decent shape is a $300–$500 job; the same length with three seasons of oxidation and salt is $700+. Quote a range on those three inputs, then confirm after a test spot on the gelcoat.

deepDive.heading: Boat detailing invoices: price by length, adjust for condition
deepDive.sub: Marine detailing is quoted by length overall (LOA) because surface area scales with it, then adjusted for how long the hull has sat in the water.

blocks.h3: Price by boat length, then by condition
paras: Put the length bracket in the line description — it removes the ambiguity when the customer measures their boat differently than you did.
Condition is the second axis. A hull that has been in the water all season needs far more compounding than one pulled and rinsed monthly, and that difference is most of the labour.
list: Under 20 ft: wash and interior clean roughly $250–$450; full detail roughly $450–$800
20–30 ft: wash and interior roughly $400–$700; full detail with compound and wax $800–$1,500
30–40 ft: full detail commonly $1,500–$2,800 depending on oxidation
Billed separately: bottom cleaning, teak treatment, canvas and isinglass, metal polishing
Winterising and shrink wrap are seasonal lines — quote them in the same document so the customer sees the annual total

blocks.h3: What goes on a marine invoice that a car invoice does not
paras: Boat work almost always happens at a marina or a customer's slip, so travel and field-service time is a real cost line rather than an overhead you absorb.
Hull condition is also a liability question: if you compound a gelcoat that is already thin, the invoice should record the condition you found it in before work started.
list: Marina or slip location on the invoice — it proves where the work happened if there is a dispute
Travel or field service charge as its own line, not folded into the package price
Condition noted before work: oxidation level, existing scratches, damaged isinglass
Water and power access fees, where the marina charges them
Photo reference on file — the cheapest defence against a claim that you caused damage you did not cause

blocks.h3: Length tiers and what each one actually costs
paras: Marine detailing is priced by length first because length drives both surface area and access. A 24-foot bowrider is a half-day job; a 40-foot sportfisher with tower, teak and multiple heads is a multi-day job at three to four times the rate. Putting the length tier on the invoice — not just the package name — is what keeps a $900 bill from looking arbitrary.

rows: Full compound, wax, topside polish, detail

blocks.h3: Saltwater, oxidation and the surcharge that is not optional
paras: Saltwater hulls need an acid wash and more time on the gelcoat than freshwater boats. Heavy oxidation — the chalky, faded finish on a boat left uncovered — can double the labour because compound has to be worked in passes rather than once. Bill oxidation as a separate line with its own hours, or you will eat the cost on every sun-baked boat that comes in.
list: Acid wash / salt removal: $3–$6 per foot, every saltwater job
Heavy oxidation removal: $8–$15 per foot, quoted after a test spot
Teak cleaning and oiling: $20–$35 per linear foot of teak
Canvas and upholstery: $40–$90 per piece, mould removal priced higher
Mould / mildew remediation below decks: hourly, with photos before and after

blocks.h3: Winterising and storage are separate invoices
paras: Cleaning a boat for winter is a different scope from a mid-season detail: the goal is to remove salt, fish blood and organic matter that will stain through the off-season, then protect surfaces before shrink-wrap or indoor storage. Owners who pay for this in the autumn rarely dispute the spring commission, because the invoice shows what was protected and when.
list: Pre-storage detail (wash, acid rinse, wax, interior dry-out): $250–$600
Engine and bilge flush: $120–$250, always its own line
Cover / shrink-wrap prep and fitting: $15–$30 per foot
